    Instructor Notes

    These notes help someone teaching this lesson live, in a workshop, class or study group. Each episode is designed to take 45 to 60 minutes of teaching and exercises. You do not need to be a security specialist, but read the episode and its worked solutions before you teach it.

    Running an episode live

    Timing

    • Plan 45 to 60 minutes for each episode, using the minutes shown on the episode page.
    • Each episode has about 20 minutes of teaching and about 35 minutes of challenges, quick check and discussion. Check the minutes on the episode page.
    • If you run short, cut the last challenge before you cut the discussion. The discussion is where learners connect the ideas to their own workplaces.

    Sticky notes

    • Give every learner a pad of sticky notes, or use a shared online board.
    • Use two colours. Green means “I follow this” and pink means “I am stuck”. Learners put the right colour on their laptop or the board at each break.
    • For challenges, learners can write one idea per note, then group the notes on a wall or board.
    • Read the pink notes at each break and answer the most common one first.

    Think-pair-share for discussions

    1. Think (1 minute). Each learner writes their own answer to the discussion question, quietly.
    2. Pair (2 minutes). Learners compare answers with a neighbour and agree on one point to share.
    3. Share (2 minutes). Pairs report back. Write the points where everyone can see them, and ask what is missing.

    Do not rush to give your own view. Ask a pair that disagrees to explain why.

    Using the Riverbend scenario

    • Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the episode that uses it, or allow 3 minutes at the start.
    • Remind learners that the page does not list problems. Finding them is the exercise.
    • If learners add facts that are not on the page, ask them to say they are assumptions.

    Challenges and solutions

    • Learners should attempt each challenge before opening the solution.
    • Solutions are worked answers. Learners’ answers may differ and still be sound. Check the reasoning, not the exact wording.

    11 Privacy law

    • Split. Week-6 video script Parts 1 to 4 (welcome, Privacy Act and APPs, data breaches, 2024 changes, Cyber Security Act). Part 5 (wider world) and Part 6 (the week’s task) are not used here. Week-6 Do 1 is split into two challenges: match ten events to the APP (15 minutes) and “Is it a data breach?” (10 minutes, built on the old Part B and on events 1 and 7). A third step in the second challenge asks why Riverbend is treated “as if” covered.
    • Riverbend and legal framing (decision). Riverbend is council-run, so the APPs and the NDB scheme do not generally bind it; state or territory law does. The episode says so in a short section, states that the exercises “treat Riverbend as if it were covered by the APPs”, and does not name a state. The ten events are recast as separate made-up Riverbend events, with details in the challenge text only. The APP mapping is the same set of principles as the source, because the principles are law content. The worked answer is fresh and uses only the event text, saying “the event does not say” where silent. The OAIC’s own page says the APPs apply to some private sector organisations and most Australian Government agencies, which supports the framing. The ransomware reporting rule is taught with a fictional furniture maker only, and is not applied to Riverbend.
    • Reading. The OAIC and cyber.gov.au pages are free and are in Go deeper. The two Acts are linked on the Federal Register of Legislation. No paid source is used in this episode.
    • Quiz items. 1 bank item (week-6 Q11) and 2 new items adapted from in-video questions. In-video question 2 (café group) was not used.
    • Discussion. None of the week-6 reflection prompts is about breaches or law, so the prompts are reflection prompt 2 (encryption, which links to the technical measures in APP 11) and one new prompt on owning up quickly. The new prompt is there because the no-blame reporting idea in the teaching text needs a prompt of its own.
    • Watch for. Learners saying the APPs bind Riverbend. Learners using APP 11 for every problem or APP 6 for marketing. Learners treating 30 days as a waiting period. Law changes: re-check dates before each run.

    12 Response and future

    • Split. Week-6 video script Part 5 (cybercrime, cyberterrorism, cyber war, the three trends), with the identity-theft response steps from Do 2. Part 6 is not used. Week-6 Do 2 is split into two challenges: Case A, the stolen wallet (15 minutes), and Case B, a message from Riverbend (10 minutes). The week-6 Do 2 worked answer and common-mistakes box give the reasoning structure; both cases are rewritten.
    • Riverbend. Case A is a Riverbend volunteer whose bag is stolen from a public bench, so no organisation is said to be at fault and card G is left out. Case B is a made-up email from Riverbend saying its member database was accessed, without saying how. The worked answer says card G may be added with a condition, and says that for a council-run library the right regulator may be a state or territory body rather than the OAIC, because card G otherwise assumes the Privacy Act. Card G in the challenge says “the regulator that covers it” for the same reason. Card E says “make a report”, not the source’s wording.
    • Reading. Goodman (2015) is paywalled, so it is cited and summarised in one short paragraph from the publisher’s description only, and is not in Go deeper. The excerpt details are still to be confirmed (see Open items), and the text does not depend on them. Publisher and edition are left out of the reference for that reason.
    • Lightly covered topics. Cyber war, cyberterrorism, the Internet of Things, big data, quantum computing and who controls the internet (governments, platforms, your own choices) are covered by a short teaching section and by discussion prompts 1, 3 (partly), 4 and 5. Reflection prompt 2 (encryption) is used in episode 11 instead.
    • Quiz items. 2 bank items (week-6 Q19 and Q23) and 1 new item on a connected device. With episode 11, the week has used 3 of the 3 allowed bank items.
    • Discussion. Week-6 reflection prompts 1, 3, 4 and 5, with a content note on the identity-theft prompt. Learners choose one, so the instructor box says to give pairs different prompts.
    • Watch for. Learners who have been through identity theft: never ask for a personal story. Learners who assume Riverbend or anyone else was at fault. Learners who name the OAIC as Riverbend’s regulator without thinking about the council.
